checkpoints: In a Redis ZSET, the member is the unique identity of an entry while the score only determines its sort order for range operations — two `ZADD` calls with the same member do not create two entries, the second call simply overwrites the score of the existing one.

The given code calls `ZADD key now now`, using the millisecond timestamp `now` as both the score and the member, so any two requests that compute the same `Date.now()` value collide on the exact same member.

Because `Date.now()` only has millisecond resolution, a burst of concurrent requests can easily produce identical timestamps, making same-member collisions realistic under load rather than a rare edge case.

When a same-millisecond collision happens, the second `ZADD` overwrites the first entry instead of adding a new one, so only one member ends up stored in the ZSET for two requests that were actually granted.

The subsequent `ZCARD` call then reports one fewer entry than the number of requests truly admitted, so the limiter compares an undercounted value against `limit` and keeps granting requests past the configured threshold.

The fix is to keep the score as `now` — so `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` window eviction still works correctly by time — while making the member unique per request, for example `${now}-${randomUUID()}` passed as the ZADD member argument.
Separating the ordering key (score) from the identity key (member) lets concurrent same-millisecond requests each occupy their own ZSET entry without breaking the time-based eviction logic.

Correctness can be verified by firing many requests concurrently within a single millisecond (e.g. `Promise.all` over `limit + 5` calls) and asserting that `ZCARD` equals the number of calls that returned `allowed: true`, with the `(limit + 1)`th request correctly denied.
